### Novel cancer therapy extends lives of terminally ill dogs, shows potential for use in human patients

###### Published: 08 Jul 2024

* * *

Image

From left: Dr Sarah Ho, A/Prof Yeo Tseng Tsai, Dr Woo Jun Yung

Researchers from the Department of Biochemistry and NUS Centre for Cancer Research (N2CR), at the Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, National University of Singapore (NUS Medicine), have been pioneering a treatment using stem cell precision engineering technology, to deliver drugs directly to tumour sites in dogs and cats with late-stage cancer and no treatment options available. In the research led by Associate Professor Too Heng-Phon, the team modified MSCs, which can seek out cancerous tumours. These modified cells carry a potent ‘kill-switch’ (cytosine deaminase) that produces a high, localised concentration of a cancer-killing drug (5-fluorouracil) in the tumour environment. The ‘kill-switch’ subsequently induces anti-cancer immunity—by activating the cancer’s innate cGAS-STING and related pathways, which activate the immune response and suppresses the tumour.

SINGAPORE - In early 2020, Ms Bridget Low, 26, noticed a lump in her toy poodle’s neck. A biopsy found the mass cancerous. The dog, Oscar, had also had daily coughing fits.

Further tests revealed a 1.5cm tumour lodged in Oscar’s left lung. Canine lung cancer is rare but deadly, and the 11-year-old poodle was given only three months to live.

But there was a possible lifeline in the form of doggy stem cells carrying cancer-killing genes. The therapy was developed at the National University of Singapore by Associate Professor Too Heng-Phon, Dr Sarah Ho and their team, based on a treatment initially meant for human patients.

Image

A scan of Oscar’s lung, showing the 1.5cm tumour in his left lung.

Oscar underwent five treatment cycles between March and September 2020, which were free, as they were part of a trial. He did not experience many side effects except for feeling lethargic and being less active, said his owner.

The dog had eight more treatment cycles ending in May 2022, when the tumour was found to have grown. Since then, it has shrunk slightly and has remained at 1.7cm. Oscar is now 14 and lives a normal life, with less frequent coughing and some asthma.

## Study title

A Pilot Study Evaluating PARP Inhibition in Combination with NSAID Therapy in Cats with Mammary Carcinoma

## Purpose of study

Feline mammary carcinoma (FMC) is an aggressive cancer with limited effective treatment options and poor long-term outcomes. In addition to exhibiting similar biologic behavior, there is a growing body of evidence indicating that many FMCs display molecular characteristics similar to triple-negative (TNBC) and basal-like subtypes of human breast cancer.

# Current Clinical Trials

We are currently seeking patients for enrollment in funded oncology clinical trials. Study goals and suitability for each patient are discussed in detail with the clients prior to enrollment. Although clinical trial enrollment may not be the best option for all patients, in many cases, clinical trial participation provides the opportunity to receive novel, cutting-edge therapies free of charge or at a reduced cost and may facilitate treatment of pets where it would not otherwise be possible due to financial constraints or lack of other therapy options. Criteria for enrollment are outlined for each tumor type below. Please direct referrals or questions to the Oncology Clinical Trials Service at 573-882-7821.

Current Trials and Studies

Bruton’s Tyrosine Kinase Inhibitor (BI705564) for Canine B‑Cell Lymphoma

The University of Missouri Veterinary Health Center is enrolling dogs in a clinical trial evaluating an investigational oral Bruton’s Tyrosine Kinase (BTK) inhibitor—BI705564—for the treatment of newly diagnosed B‑cell lymphoma. This exploratory, multicenter field study aims to assess both efficacy and safety of BTK inhibition in canine patients.

Eligibility includes:

  * Dogs >1 year old and 10–50 kg in body weight
  * Naïve, untreated B‑cell lymphoma confirmed by cytology or histology with immunophenotyping (flow cytometry)
  * At least two peripheral lymph nodes ≥2 cm in longest diameter
  * WHO stage II, III, or IV B‑cell lymphoma
  * Adequate organ function on bloodwork and urinalysis
  * Performance score of 0–1 (normal to mildly decreased activity) and life expectancy ≥1 month
  * Owner consent

Key exclusions:

  * T‑cell lymphoma or involvement of skin, GI tract, or nervous system
  * Internal‑only disease (mediastinum, liver, spleen) without peripheral lymph node enlargement
  * Prior lymphoma treatment (chemotherapy, Tanovea, Laverdia, radiation) or long‑term corticosteroids (>2 weeks)
  * Hypercalcemia, MDR1 deficiency, pregnancy/lactation, or concurrent trial enrollment

Study overview:

Dogs will receive oral BI705564 once daily for 3 months (84 days) at 5 mg/kg, with possible dose escalation to 10 mg/kg in certain cases depending on early target occupancy results.
Owners must agree to:

  * Bring their dog for all required study visits over 12 weeks
  * Administer oral medication daily as directed
  * Allow required diagnostic sampling (bloodwork, lymph node aspirates, imaging)
  * Participate in quality‑of‑life assessments

Dogs may be withdrawn at any time. If a dog passes away during the study, postmortem evaluation is requested to improve understanding of treatment effects.

Contact

For more information on this study please contact:
📧 cvmclinicaltrials@missouri.edu
Please include the subject line: BI705564 BTK Inhibitor Trial

COTC033: Repurposing Vaccine Immunity to Treat Cancers

The University of Missouri Veterinary Medical Center is enrolling patients into a clinical trial evaluating the safety and effectiveness of a new immunotherapy, the Vaccine Peptide Library (VPL), when given to dogs with cancer. Studies in dogs with cancer will complement current human trials designed to test new doses and effects of this agent.

Criteria:

  * Body weight between 15 and 60 kg
  * At the conclusion of the study, there will be a $1000 monetary gift provided towards additional treatment for your pet’s cancer.

To Participate:

  * Pet owners must be willing to transport their dog to and from the treatment center in Columbia, MO for every visit abiding by specific timelines.
  * A full screening will be performed prior to full study enrollment.
  * Participation will require a total of up to 13 weekly visits.

For more information on this study please contact: cvmclinicaltrials@missouri.edu with the subject pertaining to the trial of interest or fill out a short survey here.

Feline GI Lymphoma Radiation + Chemotherapy

The University of Missouri Veterinary Health Center is enrolling patients into a clinical trial evaluating the safety and efficacy of whole abdomen radiation therapy (WART) followed by a chemotherapy protocol (COP/Dox) in cats with spontaneous large cell GI lymphoma.  This study will seek to better understand the effects of radiation therapy prior to receiving chemotherapy for this common feline cancer.

Criteria:

  * Feline patients with high grade lymphoma in the GI tract
  * Patients must have cytologically or histopathologically confirmed lymphoma
  * Patients must not have been previously treated with chemotherapy
  * Patients cannot be FeLV or FIV positive or have severe systemic disease that would place them at higher risk with general anesthesia.
  * Patients CANNOT have evidence of lymphoma outside of the abdomen.
  * Eligibility is at the discretion of the investigator.

Benefit:

  * The cost of the radiation portion of care (WART) will be covered by the study.
  * Your pet will contribute to development of an important cancer therapy.
  * Patient will receive $1,000 stipend for use at the VHC after completion of radiation therapy

To Participate:

  * Pet owners must be willing to transport their cat to and from the treatment center in Columbia, Missouri, for every visit abiding by specific timelines.
  * A full screening including a CBC (complete blood count), serum biochemistry panel, urinalysis, thoracic radiographs (x-rays), and abdominal ultrasound will be performed prior to full study enrollment.
  * Participation will require pets to come to our clinic weekly for a minimum of eight weeks and then every 3 weeks for 5 additional visits, with radiation administered the first week only.

For more information on this study please contact: cvmclinicaltrials@missouri.edu with the subject pertaining to the trial of interest.

### Özet

Amaç: Sunulan tez çalışmasında, ADÜ Veteriner Fakültesi Cerrahi Anabilim Dalı'na getirilen kedi ve köpeklerde kanser görülme sıklığı, tipleri, güncel tedavi yöntemlerinin uygulanabilirliği ve tedavi protokollerinin başarı oranları araştırılmıştır. Böylece, kanser konusunda bakış açısının genişletilmesi, güncel ve başarı vadeden tedavi protokolleri ile hastaların refah düzeyinin arttırılması hedeflenmiştir. Gereç ve Yöntem: Çalışmada, Adnan Menderes Üniversitesi (ADÜ) Veteriner Fakültesi Cerrahi Anabilim Dalı'na 2020-2022 yılları arasında getirilen 3682 kayıtlı hastadan 19 kedi ve 90 köpek olmak üzere toplam 109 kanser hastası değerlendirilmiştir. Klinik muayene sonrası, her hastanın 3 yönlü akciğer grafisi çekilip göğüs boşluğu organları görüntülenmiştir. Metastaz şüpheli olan veya tümör lokasyonundan ötürü röntgen ile görüntüleme yapmanın yeterli olmadığı durumlarda ileri görüntüleme yöntemlerine (MR ve BT) başvurulmuştur. Hastanın öyküsü ve klinik durumuna göre belirlenen en uygun yöntemle tümörden örnekleme (biyopsi veya total rezeksiyon) yapılmıştır. Tüm cerrahi uygulamalarda tek tip anestezi protokolü; ksilazin HCL 1 mg/kg, ketamin HCL 10 mg/kg, izofluran %2 kullanılmıştır. Tümör tip tayini yapıldıktan sonra, her tümör tipine uygun en güncel ve etkin tedavi protokolü hızlıca planlanmış ve uygulanmıştır. Olguların %5,5'inde EKT, %30,2'sinde sadece cerrahi, %31,1'inde sadece kemoterapi ve %33'ünde hem cerrahi hem kemoterapi uygulaması, sağaltım yöntemi olarak kullanılmıştır. Bulgular: Adnan Menderes Üniversitesi Veteriner Fakültesi Cerrahi Anabilim Dalı'na 2020-2022 yılları arasında başvuran 3682 kayıtlı hastadan %2,9'unda (109/3682) çeşitli türde kanser belirlenmiştir. Bu 109 hastadan %82,5'inin (90/109) köpek ve %17,4'ünün (19/109) kedi olduğu belirlenmiştir. Kanser hastalarının tümör tiplerine göre dağılım; %5,5 (6/109) adenokarsinom, %22,9 (25/109) fibrom, %11,9 (13/109) hemanjiosarkom, %0,91 (1/109) kondrosarkom, %10 (11/109) lenfoma, %7,33 (8/109) enjeksiyon yeri sarkomu, %5,5 (6/109) mast hücre tümörü, %11 (12/109) osteosarkom, %17,4 (19/109) TVT, %7,33 (8/109) yassı hücreli karsinom olarak belirlenmiştir. Cinsiyet dağılımları köpeklerde; %65,5 (59/90) erkek ve %34,4 (31/90) dişi olarak belirlenirken, kedilerde; %52,6 (10/19) erkek ve %47,3 (9/19) dişi olarak belirlenmiştir. Uniform anesthesia protocol in all surgical applications; xylazine HCL 1 mg/kg (Xylazin Bio, Bioveta), ketamine HCL 10 mg/kg (Keta-Control, Doğa İlaç), isoflurane 2% (Isofluran 2%, Adeka drug) were used. After the tumor type determination was made, the most up-to-date and effective treatment protocol suitable for each tumor type was quickly planned and implemented. ECT was used as a treatment method in 5.5% of the cases, only surgery in 30.2%, only chemotherapy in 31.1%, and both surgery and chemotherapy in 33%. Results: Various types of cancer were detected in 2.9% (109/3682) of 3682 registered patients who applied to Adnan Menderes University, Faculty of Veterinary Medicine, Department of Surgery between the years 2020-2022. It was determined that 82.5% (90/109) of these 109 patients were dogs and 17.4% (19/109) were cats. Distribution of cancer patients according to tumor types; 5.5% (6/109) adenocarcinoma, 22.9% (25/109) fibroma, 11.9% (13/109) hemangiosarcoma, 0.91% (1/109) chondrosarcoma, 10% (11/109) ) lymphoma, 7.33% (8/109) injection site sarcoma, 5.5% (6/109) mast cell tumor, 11% (12/109) osteosarcoma, 17.4% (19/109) TVT, % 7.33 (8/109) were determined as squamous cell carcinoma.

Cancérologie
Le cancer est une préoccupation majeure pour les propriétaires d’animaux de compagnie. En effet, près d’un chien sur deux de plus de 10 ans en est atteint. Les avancées permanentes dans le diagnostic et le traitement des cancers en médecine vétérinaire ont permis d’améliorer l’espérance et la qualité de vie de nos animaux. Pourtant, malgré les progrès importants réalisés dans ce domaine, de nouveaux traitements sont nécessaires. Ainsi, afin que nos animaux bénéficient des nouveautés diagnostiques et thérapeutiques nous proposons la participation à des essais cliniques.

### Recrutements chiens avec tumeurs colorectales

A l’aide d’un prélèvement de selles et d’une biopsie par endoscopie, les vétérinaires de l'EnvA confirment le diagnostic de cancer colorectal chez le chien et souhaitent améliorer le dépistage précoce de cette maladie chez le chien mais aussi chez l’Homme. Une collaboration est en cours avec le Pr Tony Lefebvre, Université Lille 1.
